name: revora
description: FalkorDB-backed release agent that remembers its failures. Graph Hacks submission — Track 1 (connected data) + Track 2 (agent memory & coordination).

paragraphs: Demo video: docs/artifacts/revora-demo.mp4 — the team's 3 minute walkthrough of the live incident loop (recording script and shot list: docs/DEMOSCRIPT.md). Public replay: revora-anvitdevadiga.vercel.app; fresh execution uses a separately connected backend.

A Graph Hacks project entered in Track 2 — Agent Memory and Coordination and Track 1 — Agents That Act on Connected Data: revora operates a live HTTP gateway, measures a candidate release, recovers from an introduced incident, and uses FalkorDB memory to prevent repeating the same failed version. A second workflow demonstrates evidence-driven customer migration with invoice-preservation checks.

The problem: AI agents that operate infrastructure forget. A release agent that rolled back v7 at 2am will happily ship v7 again at 3am, and a planner agent has no durable way to see what the analyst agent measured.
features: Memory that changes behaviour. priorfailure reads the graph before routing; a match blocks the release outright. Remove the graph and the same retry serves HTTP 503 (see the acceptance ablation).

Coordination through the graph. Agents don't call each other. The analyst writes an AgentHandoff, and the planner, which may run in a separate process, reads it back from FalkorDB. Each handoff, review and decision is…
Provenance you can traverse. BASEDON, RETRIEVED and EXECUTED edges answer "why did the agent do that?" with a multi-hop query (1..4) that powers the live coordination graph in the UI.
Survives restarts. Controller route state and in-flight incidents are persisted as ReleaseControllerState, so a restarted backend resumes the incident it was handling.
